title: US Economic Resilience Comes from Consumers Borrowing from the Future
dek: Barkin explains why consumption stays strong despite high prices: consumers cut savings, skip bills, and delay loan payments to keep spending; AI investment so far is more about price hikes and crowding out than productivity gains; the Fed may face a long headwind.
why: Micro evidence a Fed official hears from the front lines: consumers sustain spending by borrowing from the future, AI construction crowds out traditional building, and tariff refunds boost profits. Useful for calibrating macro views on US inflation stickiness and AI capital spending.
who: Investors, macro traders, and Fed watchers who want to understand how US consumer resilience and AI investment affect inflation and the rate outlook.
skip: You can skip the last two minutes of program promotion and Mount Airy chit-chat; Barkin's main content has no repetition.

points.h: You can't extract forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it
points.body: Asked about Warsh's speech at Jackson Hole, Barkin said he listened carefully but explicitly refused to infer September FOMC action from it. "He himself doesn't like forward guidance, so you shouldn't look for forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it." Barkin stressed that one can discuss the economy seriously, but if you choose not to do forward guidance, you don't. This remark also addresses the market's tendency to try to extract the rate path from any Fed official comment. He described that impulse as "we can't help but want to know," but argued it should be restrained.

points.h: Consumers are borrowing money from the future
points.body: Barkin's observation: unlike the Great Recession, during the pandemic people accumulated lots of cash, stocks, and home equity, and developed a "I'm going to spend" mindset. Crucially, lower-income consumers are also "creatively finding money": switching to Walmart and dollar stores, cutting insurance, having kids move back home, not paying summer gas bills, and letting car loans run 60 days past due instead of 120—essentially "borrowing from the future." His conclusion: as long as employment and asset markets are healthy, this spending sustained by lower savings and skipped bills will continue. This micro mechanism explains the economy's "resilience" better than macro data.

points.h: Data centers are crowding ordinary construction out of the building cycle
points.body: In one week early this year, $700 billion in investment was announced; transformers, switchgear, and electricians are all in short supply. Barkin believes the construction cycle is shifting from office and multifamily to data centers and industrial. Multifamily "doesn't pencil out"—and that can't be blamed solely on rates, because in 2004-05 when rates were similarly high, they were still building plenty. He acknowledged that data center construction does push up costs for other construction, creating a "chicken-and-egg" crowding-out effect, but it's hard to say precisely to what degree. This answer soberly shows the real internal disagreement about the spillover effects of AI capex.

points.h: AI first affects hiring, not output
points.body: At every chamber of commerce and town hall, Barkin hears AI questions that are political: jobs, water, data centers. Economically, AI's productivity shock is still confined to a few replaceable scenarios like call centers, programming, and clerical work; current productivity gains come more from automation and process reengineering driven by the 2022 labor shortage. On the hiring side, employers are already using the logic of "can AI do it first, then decide whether to hire" to restrain hiring. The enthusiasm gap between firms and workers is asymmetric: bosses are proactive, employees are lukewarm. In other words, AI is currently affecting the economy by reducing employment demand rather than boosting output.

points.h: Choosing an inflation narrative is choosing a rate path
points.body: Barkin framed today's inflation as two readings. One is "65 months below target, no excuses," corresponding to Warsh's hawkish stance: inflation has been above target for a long time, and rates may not be tight enough. The other is "47 months up plus 18 months down": inflation emerged after the pandemic, and after rate hikes it had fallen to 2.3%-2.4% by March 2025, only to be pushed back up by AI, tariffs, and oil shocks. He explicitly said the second is "perfectly defensible," and "we will bring it back down later." Which narrative prevails determines whether the Fed keeps tightening or waits for shocks to fade.

points.h: Tariffs are now a stimulus because refunds have arrived
points.body: The tariff topic is quieter than six months ago, not because trade is less important, but because refunds have arrived after the Supreme Court ruling. Barkin said that over the past three or four months, businesses have been receiving refunds rather than paying extra tariffs. Steel and aluminum producers benefit from tariffs as a "price umbrella"; foreign manufacturers that ship European parts to the US for assembly are instead hurt by tariffs. Refunds are "very positive" for corporate profits, and companies use them for marketing, store renovations, and maintaining hiring, so there is a stimulative effect, but the pass-through to prices is "very targeted," not systemic. This explains why people aren't complaining much about tariffs now.

points.h: Data center tax base buys no political goodwill
points.body: Local residents resent data centers because, unlike factories, they don't bring workers' kids to play sports with local children; the tax base benefits touted by economic developers lack political resonance. Barkin half-joked that they should name an elementary school after Microsoft or Google to win hearts. He admitted he doesn't know how large data centers will become; AI footprint, data center footprint, and energy demand could all be significantly under- or overestimated. If political backlash leads to underbuilding, it will drag on growth; if overbuilding, it will add to inflation. This is an uncertainty not yet incorporated into the policy framework.

points.h: AI could be inflationary or deflationary; don't bet early
points.body: On whether AI will bring a productivity boom and raise the neutral rate R-star, Barkin is cautious. He said the AI path one, two, or three years out has an "extremely wide range," and could manifest as inflation or deflation, with 18 versions in between. Until there is enough confidence, policy cannot be based on assumptions. He also responded to Warsh's view: different AI model simulations point to completely opposite rate directions. Therefore, he hinted the Fed should wait for data rather than put AI productivity into the dot plot ahead of time. This stance is a warning to those betting on a higher R-star.

quotes.text: And I'm not saying inflation is definitely heading in the wrong direction. It's just not in the right place.
So people are finding ways to effectively borrow from the future, savings rates down.
I don't think it's ridiculous to imagine that 10 years later you might have a bunch of factors that would bring inflation up.
And if what's happening is that picture is swamping the narrative, then we're going to think differently about the picture.
Well, I'm definitely 100% insistent on getting inflation under control.
Those big box retailers, they're truly our strongest soldiers in the fight against inflation, holding the line on prices on behalf of the customer.
I think the anecdote doesn't, everyone likes a good story, but it doesn't really move policy.
